title: NCR Patterns at ADW
body: Nineteen NCRs on file and the same names, locations, and timing keep repeating — Sadiq Ali got NCR'd again six days after his first, and two separate NCR numbers have now been issued twice to different people. When a corrective action isn't verified and the register isn't controlled, the same breach just resurfaces under a new date.
keyPoints: NCRs cluster at shift transitions — late day shift (16:00-17:20) and pre-dawn (04:16-06:30). That's when supervision is thinnest: handover focus pulls supervisors off the floor, and the day-shift supervisor isn't on site yet. Treat those windows as higher-risk, not routine.

Location concentration tracks the highest-stakes ground — Stage 4, Stage 6, and the ROM pad account for most of the corpus. If you're walking those areas during a shift change, you're walking into the exact conditions that produce NCRs.

A corrective action only holds if someone checks it happened. The WL-24 light-damage NCR fixed the gap by making the end-of-shift walkaround a signed checklist item with weekly spot-checks — not just a toolbox talk. Verbal expectations without a verification step get skipped.

"Verify before refuse" applies to equipment, not just people. The Syukur/DT110 case cost ~1,500 tons because an operator refused a truck based on a transmission complaint from three months earlier, without re-inspecting it after repair. A refusal needs a fresh inspection, not a memory.

NCR numbers must be unique or the whole trail breaks. Two number collisions this year (26-012, 26-021) mean two different findings get conflated in any audit or closeout count — check the number before you file, not after.
apply: At shift change near the ROM pad or Stage 4/6, confirm the outgoing operator actually did their end-of-shift walkaround and sign-off before you accept the handover as clean.
